translations.text: A eulogy delivered by Saint Apa Acacius, bishop of Caesarea, in the martyr’s shrine built in the name of Saint Mercurius, on the day of his holy commemoration, which is the twentieth day of the month of Hathor. He praised the many mighty deeds and wonders that took place through the holy martyr Saint Mercurius. In the peace of God. May his holy blessings be with us all together. Amen.

Truly, light has dawned for the righteous, for this Saint Mercurius, according to [?], as the sacred psalmist said—the father of Christ according to the flesh, the righteous king, David the singer of hymns.
He cries out, he cries out in his sweet voice, singing with his lyre and the plectrum in his hand, saying, “Light has dawned for the righteous.”
And again, “Light has dawned in the darkness for those who are upright in heart.”
Christ himself said in the Gospel, “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.”
Saint Mercurius [?] you see [?] boundless [?], for you were a pagan before you knew Christ well.
And when he had armed himself, he went out to war against the barbarians.
He was before [?], the lawless king, as commander of the army.
He held the arrows and the bow with which he would slaughter the barbarians.

But the angel of the Lord came down from heaven and gave him a sword, saying, “Strike the barbarians [?].” [?] “We must show great goodwill toward them and give them honor and glory according to their worth, with libations and sacrifices, in accordance with the good things they have previously done for us.

We command that the doors of all the temples be opened in every city and every village, from the Roman Empire southward to Philae and the lands of Kush, and that incense be offered to the revered gods and their worship be performed with great zeal.

No Christian is to appear anywhere, and the provincial governors are to pursue these Christians everywhere, whether bishop, priest, reader, monk, layperson, man, woman, soldier, civilian, or official—in short, every kind of person—by the authority of my empire, so that they sacrifice to the revered gods.
And whoever opposes my command is to be handed over to great and varied tortures until they die.”

Then Decius, the lawless king, commanded the herald to proclaim throughout the whole city, “Notice is given to all of you people, whether soldiers, civilians, or people of any kind and any age: Come, all of you, [?] the temple of the gods and offer sacrifices to them.” They lit incense at the entrance of the temple and offered them sacrifices and incense, calves, sheep, and birds. The sky was filled with smoke from the stench of their sacrifices.
And there was great turmoil among the Christians. They were pursued, beaten, and dragged into the gateways and hidden places, and they were forced to offer sacrifices.

There were great disturbances everywhere, for the tyrant had ordered every kind of terrifying instrument of torture to be placed before him, so that the Christians would see them and become afraid: sharpened swords, iron beds, devices for stretching sinews, razors for cutting out tongues, cleavers, sharp [?], bronze cauldrons full of boiling lead, other bronze cauldrons full of pitch, saw wheels, and all the other terrifying instruments of torture.

For that godless king was saying, “Whoever opposes my command, I will gouge out his eyes, cut out his tongue, extract his marrow, saw off his toes, and take out his brain. The rest of his body I will give to the fire, and it will consume it.”
When the devout people saw these things, great faintheartedness overtook them. They became afraid and gave up.

Each person was handing over his neighbor to death. Fathers were handing over their children to death, forgetting their natural love. Brothers were dragging one another away, throwing one another down, and handing one another over. There was great turmoil
for everyone who confessed the name—the name of Jesus.
There was a brave young man in the army whose name was Mercurius. He was enrolled in the Martysios regiment and feared God.
He was very handsome in appearance, and the whole army loved him because of his skill.
[?] He was a native of the region of Cappadocia. He had been a Christian since childhood, along with his parents.
He was brave in battle, and God was with him in everything he did.
When the tribune saw that he was advancing in his rank and in military proficiency, he made him primicerius over his regiment.
When the king saw the young man’s bravery, he loved him and kept him close to himself, consulting him about the affairs of the palace.
After these things, while the persecution was spreading, a barbarian nation rose up against the Romans.
Emperor Decius and the entire senate were at a loss because of the great crisis and helplessness that had arisen suddenly.
The barbarians fought against them in order to take Greater Armenia from them, which lay within their borders, between them and the Romans.
Emperor Decius ordered the military units and all the Roman regiments to assemble, so that they could go out to war and fight the barbarians.
Then the king organized the divisions and regiments and marched out to war against the barbarians.
He crossed the Euphrates, the great river that lies within the borders of Armenia. He established the [?] opposite the barbarians and remained facing them with his army.
It was at that time that the bravery of this noble man became apparent: Saint Mercurius, who was truly faithful, and the primicerius of the Martyros regiment.
For he was a man whose devotion to God was complete, and he lived with every kind of godliness.
The word of God was always sweeter in his mouth than honey.
One night, while he was sleeping among the troops, after he had finished praying, he dozed off for a little while.

Suddenly an angel of the Lord stood over him, touched his side, and woke him. The angel had a sword in his right hand. His appearance was frightening, and he wore a marvelous robe. When Saint Mercurius saw him, he was very afraid.
The angel addressed him, saying, “Mercurius!” He replied, “Here I am, my lord.”
Mercurius opened his eyes, and when he saw the angel, he was afraid, thinking that he was one of the emperor’s officials or a military commander.
He held out to him the sword he was carrying, drawn in his hand, and said to him, “Take this drawn sword that is in my hand, for with it you will strike down the entire force of the barbarians.
For I am the commander-in-chief of the Lord’s army.
I have come to help you and your fellow soldiers who believe in the Lord Jesus Christ.
Now, then, prevail and be strong, for I am with you until your struggle is completed in peace.
Look, [?] the time has come, and the contest lies before you.
Fight so that you may receive your strength. An athlete does not receive a crown unless he competes properly, and the farmer who works hard is the first to receive a share of the crops.
Now, then, listen to the words I am saying to you, and do not delay in turning to the Lord your God. For a great struggle awaits you, and you will become a courageous martyr.”

For your martyrdom will become known throughout the whole world. Everyone who hears of it will marvel at your courage and give glory to God because of the mighty deeds, wonders, and acts of courage that the Lord your God has performed for you.
Great tortures will be inflicted on you by the lawless emperor, along with great suffering. But persevere, and you will receive the imperishable crown.
And everyone who is worthy to touch your body—we will save him.

Even if they are in any kind of distress, whether in a court, in a deserted place, in danger at sea, on the river, or in trouble that torments them, whoever remembers your name in faith and calls upon you will be saved.

Whoever builds a shrine in your name and gives an offering in your name on the day of your commemoration, I will place my blessing and lasting prosperity upon their dwelling, and I will never let them lack anything.
Whoever writes the book of your martyrdom, I will tear up the written record of his sins. I will never remember any of the things he has done, and I will grant him to you as a son in my kingdom.
Look, I have granted you three crowns: one for wealth, one for the sufferings you will endure for my name, and another for your virginity.
Be victorious and be strong, for I am with you.
After the archangel Michael had said these things to him, he ascended to heaven in glory.
When those around him saw the great vision that had appeared, they became like dead people.

The next day, Emperor Decius ordered his army to arrange the battalions and regiments. After they had equipped themselves with their full battle armor, they took their positions for war against the barbarians.
Then the truly courageous Saint Mercurius charged against the multitude of barbarians. He went into their midst through the power of God, who was with him.
He raised his eyes to heaven and saw the archangel Michael in the form of an army commander.

A sword was held firmly in his right hand, and he extended it toward him, saying, “Take courage and grasp this sword. Charge against the barbarians and slaughter them in the name of Christ, who gives you strength.”
Saint Mercurius stretched out his hand and took the sword from the angel Michael. He charged against the multitudes of barbarians.

He slaughtered them mercilessly in the name of Christ, until his hand stuck to the sword because of the great amount of blood, as he struck down the barbarians amid exceedingly great and severe suffering that day.
The rest fled and disappeared, as though a fire from heaven had consumed them.
When the emperor saw the bravery that Saint Mercurius had shown through the power of God, who was with him, he rejoiced greatly over the victory and the triumph that had come to the Romans.
The emperor bestowed great honors and abundant riches on Saint Mercurius. He [?] and made him commander of the Martusion regiment.

After these things, Emperor Decius ordered all the armies, battalions, and regiments, together with the commanders, generals, patricians, and the entire Roman senate, to assemble at the temple of Apollo and offer sacrifices.

Then, when the blessed Mercurius saw the great delusion that had taken hold of the emperor and the army through the devil, he withdrew from them and went into his house. He pleaded with the Lord, saying, “Lord Almighty, Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on your creature, whom you created, and scatter the stumbling block that the devil has cast into the heart of all humanity.”
And give steadfastness to the heart of the people and of everyone who fears your holy name.
Lord, strengthen your churches so that everyone may believe in your holy name. Glory to you and to your good Father and to the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.
When the emperor came to the entrance of the temple, his entire army gathered so that they might all offer sacrifices, each one according to his rank.
The turn of Saint Mercurius also came for him to offer sacrifice, but they did not find him among the army.

And when the emperor searched for him, he found him sitting in his house in sackcloth and ashes, grieving deeply over the great division that had come upon the whole inhabited world through the devil.

Then some men from his regiment approached the emperor and slandered the blessed Mercurius, saying, “Our lord the emperor, live forever! Your honored authority commanded people of every kind to offer sacrifices to the honored gods.

Now, look: those close to you and those attached to you despise your honored decree. Mercurius, who holds authority in your kingdom—you exalted him and granted him the rank of count over the regiment.
And since the entire Roman army obeyed him, honored him, and submitted to him because of the great honor you bestowed on him,

look, he despises your authority! He did not gather with us at the temple to offer sacrifices to the gods. Instead, he went to his house, stripped himself of his rank, disgraced the glory of the Romans, and defiled the holy laws.
We found him inside his house, sitting in sackcloth and ashes, praying with tears to the Lord his God.

He is also persuading everyone to turn away from the worship of the gods. He has made them follow Jesus the Nazarene, whom they crucified, saying, ‘This is God; he created heaven and earth.’ In this way he has made everyone withdraw from the gods.”

The emperor said to those who were saying these things, “Are these things you are telling me about Mercurius, who is attached to me, true—that he despises my gods? In any case, let two officials who are here go and summon him, so that I may find out whether these things you are telling me about him are true or not.”
Then they brought the blessed Mercurius before the emperor Decius.
His eyes were full of tears, and he wore a humble garment. They made him stand before the emperor.
When he saw him in his humble appearance, he shook his head, puzzled over what had happened.
Then he spoke to him, saying, “Mercurius, tell me what has happened to you, and why you have despised this great honor and the rank
that I gave you. I made you worthy of the gods’ care, yet you have considered the rank I gave you above all the rest of the army to be nothing.
“Now, then, tell me through whom this delusion came upon you.”
The Roman army gathered at the temple to offer sacrifices to the gods, as is right. But you alone separated yourself from the regiment.
In any case, tell me who you are, what country you come from, and whether your parents called you by this name.”
The blessed Mercurius answered and said to the emperor, “If you want to know who I am and what religion I belong to, listen to my ancestry. In this world, I am from Cappadocia.”

In truth, I am from the heavenly Jerusalem, the capital city of the saints. The name my parents first gave me was Philopator, which means ‘one who loves his father.’ When I became a soldier, the chief officer of my regiment named me Mercurius.
I am the servant of Jesus Christ, my Lord, the Son of the living God.
When the emperor heard these things, he cried out in great anger.
He shook his head, saying, ‘Mercurius, give up this defiance and this madness. Go into the temple and sacrifice to the great god Apollo.’
‘Then go to your regiment, to your fellow soldiers, and receive your rank as before.’

Saint Mercurius said before the lawless emperor, ‘Let this be clear to you, lawless emperor: I will not sacrifice to your Apollo, a worthless idol, and abandon my God, who created heaven, earth, and everything.’
‘For I am a Christian.’
‘Openly, I will renounce military service in this world. I have no need of your rank. I am the servant of Christ Jesus, the Son of the living God.’

The emperor Decius answered him, saying, ‘Mercurius, until now I did not believe what your accusers told me about you. For I know that they accused you out of envy, when they saw the great honor I gave you in the midst of the whole regiment and the army.’
‘Now, then, obey me and sacrifice to the gods.’
‘Do not let this matter force me to forget the affection I had for you, strip you of your rank, and inflict severe punishments on you.’
The blessed man answered the emperor, saying, ‘Friendship with this world is nothing; it is hostility toward God.’
‘And honors of this kind are temporary.’
‘But God's glory lasts forever. Now, then, do not trouble yourself in vain. For I am a Christian. I will not sacrifice to your abominable gods. So do to me whatever you wish.’

Decius said to him, ‘Mercurius, sacrifice! Do not die a dreadful death.’ The blessed Mercurius said to him, ‘Let one statement satisfy you, emperor: I will certainly not obey you by serving foreign gods and abandoning my God, Jesus Christ.’

When Decius heard these things, he became very angry. He ordered them to strip him of his clothes, and ten soldiers to stretch him out and beat him with raw oxhide whips until the ground beneath him was wet with his blood.
The emperor Decius said to him, ‘Mercurius, you have tasted the beginning of the tortures, how terrible they are. Will you sacrifice or not?’
The blessed Mercurius answered, “As long as I have my Lord Jesus Christ helping him, I am not troubled by your tortures.”
‘For I am the servant of my Lord Jesus Christ, who helps me. He is the king of those in heaven and those on earth.’
When the emperor Decius heard these things, he said, ‘Mercurius, obey me and sacrifice to the gods. Escape severe tortures, so that you do not die miserably.’
‘Until now I have spared you and been patient with you.’
‘For I do not want to harm you, especially since you became my companion by fighting for me in the war.’
‘Obey me and sacrifice to the gods.’
‘Do not destroy your youth through cruel tortures.’
‘I have compassion for your youth and for your friendship.’

The blessed Mercurius answered, “Every suffering that comes upon me because I confess God is worth more to me than a holy reward. For the sufferings of the present time are not worthy of the glory that will be revealed to us.”

When Emperor Decius heard these words, he said, “If you have set your heart on foolish words and have regarded the honors of the Romans as nothing, refusing to sacrifice to the rightful gods according to the decrees of the senate, and have not obeyed the laws of the emperors, I too will punish you according to your foolishness. Then I will see whether the God in whom you have trusted can rescue you from my hands.”
Saint Mercurius answered the emperor, saying, “It is written in the holy Apostle: ‘Who can separate us from the love of God?
Is it trouble, or distress, or persecution, or hunger, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written: For your sake we are being killed all day long.’
For we are convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor rulers nor powers, neither present things nor things to come, will be able to separate us from the love of Christ.”
When the blessed Mercurius said these things, Emperor Decius became angry. He ordered them to put him on the rack and scrape him.
The executioners scraped him until the bone of his spine was exposed.

But the blessed man did not stop blessing God. He said, “Lord Jesus Christ, the only Son of the Father, born of the holy Virgin Mary, who took flesh from the true dove to redeem the whole race of Adam and free us from slavery to sin, I thank you because you have made us worthy of your great goodness.
Listen to me today.
I am your servant Mercurius.
Make me worthy of your holy calling, a sharer in your holy sufferings, and a faithful witness to your divinity.
Now then, my Lord, do not abandon me, and do not turn away from me, for troubles are pressing upon me and snares have fallen upon me.
But give me strength, my Lord, so that I may finish my struggle in peace. Do not let my enemies rejoice over me, and do not let them say among the nations, ‘Where is their God?’”
While he was saying these things, a voice came to him, saying, “Take courage, my soldier Mercurius. Endure, my chosen mighty warrior.
For I am with you, strengthening you, and I will be with you as your protector, helping you in every suffering you endure in my name. Do not grow weak or lose heart before the tortures.
I am with you, strengthening you until you finish your struggle with courage.”
Immediately the archangel Michael greeted him and marked his whole body with a seal.
Immediately the rack split in two, and the bonds with which he was bound came loose. He sprang up and stood, with no injury in him, but he was giving glory to God.

When the emperor saw what had happened, he was filled with anger. He said, “Since this man has said, ‘We have a suit of armor of [?],’ I order them to stretch him out on four stakes and suspend him between heaven and earth, a cubit above the ground.”
When they had done this to him, the emperor said, “Where now are the weapons in which you trust? By Zeus, the greatest of the great gods, they have stretched you out completely!”

The holy man looked up to heaven and said, “Lord, help me. I am your servant.” Again the emperor ordered them to scourge his body with tough cords and whips, and afterward to spread burning coals beneath him so that he would burn little by little. But the fire was extinguished by the righteous man’s blood as it flowed down.
But the holy man recovered his strength with great fortitude during this further torture.
The emperor Decius had him taken away, lest he die too quickly, and they hurriedly threw him into a dark place.
The soldiers carried him away half dead, with only a little breath remaining in him, thinking that he had died.
A little later, at that very hour, an angel of the Lord appeared to him and said, “Peace to you, victorious warrior!”
When he had received this, the angel healed the wounds on his body and set him on his feet, healthy. Once he had risen, he stood glorifying God, who helped him.
After this, the emperor ordered them to bring him before the tribunal.
When the emperor [?] him, he said to him, “They took you away from me half dead. How is it that you are walking now? Perhaps there is not even a wound on your body!”
Then he ordered the guards who stood there to examine his body.
They said to the emperor, “By your power, O pious emperor, his entire body is healthy. There is no injury in it, as though they had never touched him at all.”
Decius himself said, “He will certainly say, ‘It is Christ who healed me.’ Did you bring a physician into the prison to treat him?”
They said, “By your honored Majesty, who rules over the whole inhabited world, no human healer has healed him.”
“But [?] we do not know how he will die while he is alive, or how to make him stop. For the magic of the Christians is a hard wood that does not rot or decay.”
Yet today he stands here healthy.
The emperor was filled with anger and said to him, “Tell me truthfully who healed you without magic.”

Saint Mercurius answered, “My Lord Jesus Christ, the physician of souls and bodies—it is he who granted me healing. As he said, sorcerers, those who summon spirits, and idol worshipers are strangers to him. He will bind them with bonds that cannot be undone and hand them over to the fire of Gehenna, because they did not acknowledge the God who created them.”
He said, “I will wear out your body with harsh tortures. Let me see whether the Christ in whom you believe will heal you.”
Saint Mercurius said, “I trust in my Lord Jesus Christ that even if you inflict many punishments on me, you will not be able to shake me.”
“For he said, ‘Do not fear those who will kill your bodies but have no power to kill your souls.’
“‘Rather, fear the one who has power to destroy both your soul and your body in Gehenna.’”

Then the emperor ordered them to bring a glowing-hot iron and put it beneath his elbows, and to place burning torches beneath his sides. When they did this, instead of smoke, a sweet fragrance arose and spread to everyone in that place. Although they tortured him still more, he neither groaned nor wept. The emperor said to him, “Where is your physician now? Let him come and treat you! For you said that he has the power to raise the dead.”
But Saint Mercurius said to him, “Do whatever you wish, for you have authority over my body. But God is the master of my soul. Even if you destroy my body, my soul will remain imperishable.”
Again the emperor ordered them to hang him upside down and bring a large stone and fasten it to his neck, so that he would choke and die quickly.
But God's power and grace dwelt in the martyr, and he endured this torture for a long time.

When Emperor Decius saw that the martyr bore the punishments steadfastly and that no torture had overcome him, he ordered them to remove the stone from his neck and bring a bronze whip with four thongs and beat him until the earth was soaked with his blood.
But the noble man withstood this further torture, firm as a stone of adamant.
And he said, “I thank you, my Lord, because you have made me worthy to suffer for your holy name.”

When the emperor saw that his resolve was unshakable and that he could not persuade him to offer sacrifice, he took counsel. Since he was in a hurry to go to Rome, he pronounced sentence on him, ordering that he be punished with the sword. He said, “Mercurius has insulted the gods and despised the sacred decrees of our wisdom. He has treated our authority as nothing. I order that he be taken to the city in Cappadocia and beheaded there, with everyone watching him.”
For anyone who has received honor from the emperor, if he opposes his command, will be subjected to blows, and finally he will be handed over to the sword.
Those appointed to carry him lifted him up, put him on a pack animal, and tied him onto it, because the martyr's body had fallen apart on every side. He had become like a corpse.
They traveled along the long road, and after a few days they reached the city of Caesarea. Then they lowered him down little by little.

The Lord stood over him and said to him, “Mercurius, come and rest beside me, since you have finished your race and kept the faith. Receive your crown of glory, which has been appointed for you to inherit.”

When the Lord appeared to the martyr, he gained strength. He said to those attending him, “Quickly do what you have been ordered to do. May the Lord, who calls everyone to repentance, make you worthy of his grace.”
For he is rich and freely gives gifts, without begrudging them, to those who come to him.
After he said these things, they beheaded him. He completed the good confession of our Savior on the twenty-fifth of November, that is, Athor.

A great miracle took place, worthy of being remembered. After the martyr had reached his end, his body became white like snow, giving off a sweet fragrance like choice incense. Because of this sign, many people became Christians.
They laid the saint in a publicly visible shrine, where many miracles and healings take place.
Glory to God the Father, and to his only Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, and to the Holy Spirit, now and always, forever and ever. Amen.
The martyrdom of Saint Mercurius, the commander and holy martyr of Christ, which he completed on this day, the twenty-fifth of the month of Athor. In peace. 99.

In the time of Decius and Valerian, when they were emperors in the great city of Rome, they issued a decree and a joint resolution requiring everyone everywhere to sacrifice to the gods and pour out libations to them.

They summoned all the senators and laid before them what they had decided in this joint resolution. When they found that the senators were of one mind with them, they rejoiced greatly, saying, “We thank our immortal gods, who have revealed this unanimous decision.” And at that very hour
they ordered a decree to be issued, written as follows in an imperial letter, in this form:
Decius and Valerian, the sovereign and pious emperors, together with all the senators of Rome, write to those who live everywhere: We have considered it necessary to inform you of what pleases us.

Since a long time ago we discovered that the gods of our ancestors uphold our empire and grant good things to everyone under our authority, we know their kindness toward us and their gifts, just as they have said. Indeed, through them we have enjoyed victory over all the nations. Not only that, but they have supplied us with abundant crops through the temperate climate. Therefore, we and all the senators have unanimously issued this decree with great earnestness: everyone everywhere, free people and slaves, soldiers and civilians, must bring sacrifices to the gods and offer them prayers and supplications.

But if anyone of his own accord rejects our sacred decree, which we have unanimously ordered, our authority commands that such a person be brought [?] into a dark prison and subjected to severe tortures.
But whoever obeys our command will receive great honor from us.
“But if he disobeys us and our decree, he will be handed over to punishment by the sword, or to death by [?], or he will be given as food to the wild beasts and the birds.”
“Christians, especially, will be subject to a sentence of this kind.”
Those who obey our decree will live in happiness.

When the emperor's command was proclaimed, the whole city of Rome was filled with turmoil and fear. Not only that, but all the other cities were also thrown into turmoil, because this same decree had been sent to them. The officials in each city ordered the people to carry out quickly what they had been commanded to do.
At that time, the barbarians began a war against the Romans.
Changing their appearance, they too prepared their army to wage war against them. They ordered the regiments in every district and every city to come and assist them.
When they came from each of the cities, eagerly prepared, the regiment of those called Martysion also came. They were stationed in Armenia Prima under a tribune whose name was Sardonicus.
Decius went out to war, while Valerian remained in Rome, administering the affairs of the empire.
The war intensified between the barbarians and the Romans, and they stood against one another.

After they had continued in this way for many days, a man named Mercurius, who belonged to the regiment of those called the Martenses, saw a tall, radiant man wearing glorious clothes. He held a drawn sword in his right hand and said to him, “Mercurius, do not be afraid or be alarmed.”
For I have been sent to help you and to reveal you as a victor.
Take this sword from me and go out against the barbarians. When you defeat them, do not forget the Lord your God.
When this man fell into a trance, he thought that the one speaking with him was one of the emperor's high officials.

When he took the sword and was filled with the Holy Spirit, he went into their midst and killed their leader and many others with him. His arm grew weary from striking, and because of the great amount of blood, his hand stuck fast to the sword's handle.
This was how the barbarians fled and were slaughtered before the Romans.
Then, when Emperor Decius learned of this mighty man's courage, he summoned him and gave him a position of honor. He made him a general and commander over his entire army.

Decius, thinking that he had won the war through the providence of the gods, rejoiced greatly and showered the soldiers with a great deal of money. That day, the regiments were sent to their own stations.
He himself held celebrations in every city through which he passed on his way to Rome.
One night, while the army was asleep, an angel stood over Mercurius in the form of the man whom he had seen during the war. He prodded his side and woke him.

When he saw him, he became afraid. But the angel said to him, “Do you remember the words I spoke to you during the war, Mercurius? Take care not to forget the Lord your God, for you must fight well for his name and receive your crown of victory in the kingdom of heaven, which he has prepared for all who love him.” When he had said this, he withdrew from him immediately.
When the blessed man came to his senses, he remembered the words and marveled at the power of God’s love for humanity. For he had heard about the Christians’ faith through his parents.

His father was Gordian, who was the chief officer of this same regiment. The young man was approaching twenty-five years of age. For he had often heard his father say, “Blessed is the one who serves as a soldier under the King of heaven. He will grant him great, incomparable honors, and he will fight on his behalf against his enemies.”
For that King is the one who created everything by his word.

He established the sky like a vault and adorned it with shining stars, and the earth with beautiful, fragrant flowers to bring people comfort and healing. He also made the sea so that ships could sail on it, and made it a place where fish could be nourished.

And he is the one who is coming to judge the living and the dead and give each person according to their deeds. When Saint Mercurius recalled in his heart his father's words and the revelation he had seen, he became deeply troubled. He began to weep and sigh, saying, “Woe to him! I am the sinner, like a fruitless branch that has withered, having no root in the knowledge of God's glory.”
While he was still speaking, the emperor immediately sent two of those called silentiaries, together with some others, to summon him, because he was his adviser.
He asked to be excused from going, saying, “My body is weak.” The emperor said nothing that day. But the next day Decius again sent for him in the same way.
When he came to him, they consulted with one another about the matter at hand.
The emperor said to him, “Let us go, Mercurius, to the great temple of Artemis and offer sacrifices to her.”
When the emperor set out, a large crowd followed him.
But the blessed Mercurius turned back and hid in the praetorium.
Someone accused him before the emperor, saying, “Great, powerful, victorious, and pious emperor, chosen by the gods to govern the entire Roman Empire, allow me to speak, and listen to me kindly.”

“Mercurius, whom your powerful right hand exalted and whom you honored in the Roman Empire, did not come with us in accordance with your command to sacrifice in the temple of the great Artemis and make offerings to her according to the authoritative command.”

The emperor replied, “Who is this?” He said, “Mercurius, the man to whom you granted victory and greatness yesterday and the day before, down to this very day, and whom you raised to a rank of even greater authority.”
“Not only has this man disobeyed Your Greatness, but he has also [?] many who worship the gods.”
“If you question him, you will learn the full extent of what I have told you.”

But Decius said, “Perhaps envy of the man arose in your heart, and you said these things. But I will not believe you unless I establish the truth with certainty and see the matter for myself, face to face.”
“For seeing with the eyes is considered more reliable than hearing with the ears.”
“So be silent now, and do not say anything more against the man. If you accused him out of envy, as I told you, understand that you will be liable to a severe punishment.”
“But if what you have said proves true, you will receive great gifts from us, since you are of one mind with us toward the gods and toward the emperors.”

He ordered Saint Mercurius to be brought with the honor previously due to him. When he came before him, the emperor said to him, “Mercurius, was it not I who gave you this great honor and this rank, making you a general among all my officers because of your courage and the victory the gods granted us in the war? How have you turned the great affection I have for you into bitter hatred, and reduced those great honors to nothing, despising the gods so completely, as we have been informed, abandoning piety?” Then the truly noble soldier of Christ stripped himself of the old self and its deeds, according to the words of Paul the apostle, and put on the new self, which had been created within him according to God through baptism. The saint answered in a joyful and courageous voice, “Keep this sort of honor for yourself. For although I went out to war and fought, it was not I who won, but the Lord, who granted me the Lord [?].
“Nevertheless, take back your honors, as you have said. For I came naked from my mother’s womb, and I will go away naked again.”
After saying this, he took off his military cloak, unfastened his belt, and threw them down at the emperor’s feet. He shouted, “I am a Christian! Hear it, all of you: I am a Christian!”
Then Decius became like someone stunned. He gazed into his face for a long time, marveling at his appearance and his youthful beauty.
The blessed man was very handsome in appearance, with a radiant complexion and reddish hair, adorned with every kind of beauty
and strength. Many looked at him in amazement.
After this, the emperor Decius shook his head and ordered him to be thrown into prison, saying, “Let the man who did not appreciate honor now experience humiliation.”
He said this thinking that he could change his devout resolve. But as Christ’s martyr was being taken to prison, he rejoiced and exulted in the Spirit, giving glory to God.
That night an angel stood over him and said to him, “Mercurius, take courage, and do not fear the tyrant’s threats.

“Believe in Christ, who is God, and confess that he is Christ, who is God, for he is able to save you from every affliction.” The martyr himself became still stronger. These were the things the angel said to him when he appeared to him.

The next day Decius sat on the judgment seat and ordered the blessed man to be brought before him. He said to him, “Does this sort of honor that you have received from me suit you—the humiliation you chose for yourself?”
The blessed man answered, “It suits me far better.
“For I have received a rank that cannot perish.” The emperor said to him, “Tell me your ancestry and your city.
“For I know which rank you belong to.”
Saint Mercurius said to him, “If you want to know my ancestry and my city, I will tell you about them.”
My father according to the flesh came from Scythia. His name was Gordian, and he served as a soldier in the regiment of the Martenses.
At that time he was the commander of that same military unit.
“My true Father is God, and my city is the heavenly Jerusalem, the city of the great King.”

The emperor said to him again, “Were you given the name Mercurius by your parents, or was it the soldiers who gave it to you?” Saint Mercurius said, “My father called me Philopator, which means ‘one who loves his parents.’
“But when I became a soldier, I was named Mercurius by the tribune.”

The emperor said to him, “Mercurius, what do you say? Will you obey our decree, which we have published for everyone, worship the gods, and receive your former honor and glory, or not? What do you say? Tell us quickly, since you know that you were brought here for this matter.”
The martyr answered, saying, “I came here to overcome you and your father Satan, through whom every evil has come about.
If I win, I will be crowned by the true judge of the contest, my Lord Jesus Christ. So do whatever you wish quickly, and do not delay.
For I have the full armor of God and the shield of faith. Through these I will overcome your schemes and all your deceitful tricks against me.”

Then the emperor was filled with anger and said, “Since this man says, ‘I have a suit of armor [?],’ although he stands naked, I command that he be stretched out with four ropes and suspended between heaven and earth, a cubit above the ground.”
When they had done this to him, the emperor said, “Where are your weapons now, the ones you rely on? By the great god Zeus, they have stretched you out thoroughly!”
The saint looked up to heaven and said, “My Lord, help me, your servant!”

Again the emperor ordered them to lash his body with stiff rods instead of whips, and afterward to spread burning coals beneath him so that he would burn little by little. The flame of the fire was extinguished by the righteous man’s blood as it flowed down.
But the saint endured this great torture with great fortitude.

Decius ordered them to untie him so that he would not die quickly, to put him in a dark place, and to secure him there immediately. The soldiers lifted him up, half dead, with only a little breath remaining in him, thinking that he would die.
The soldiers lifted him up, half dead, with only a little breath remaining in him, thinking that he would die.
A little later, at that very moment, the angel of the Lord appeared to him and said, “Peace to you, victorious fighter!”
When he had said this, he healed the wounds on his body and set him on his feet, healthy, so that he rose, stood, and gave glory to God, who had helped him.
After this, he ordered them to bring him before the judgment seat. When the emperor saw him, he said to him, “They carried you away from me half dead.
How are you walking now? Could it really be that there is no wound on your body?” Then he ordered the guards standing there to examine his body.
They said to the emperor, “By your power, O pious emperor, his whole body is healthy, with no injury on it, like someone whom no one has touched at all with a finger.”
Decius himself said, “He will certainly say, ‘It was Christ who saved me and healed me.’
Did you bring a doctor into the prison to treat him?”
They said, “By your honored majesty, which rules over the whole inhabited world, no one treated him.
On the contrary, we thought he would die. How he is alive now, or how he recovered, we do not know.”
He said to them, “You know how powerful the Christians’ magic is.
How is it that yesterday he was a corpse, but today he is standing, healthy?”
Filled with anger, he said to him, “Tell me truthfully who healed you, apart from magic.”
Saint Mercurius answered, “My Lord Jesus Christ, the true physician of our souls and our bodies—it is he who wishes to grant me healing, just as I said.

But sorcerers, conjurers, and idol worshipers are strangers to him. He will bind them with bonds that cannot be undone and hand them over to the fire of Gehenna, because they did not acknowledge the true God who created them.”
The emperor said, “Then I will destroy your body with severe tortures.
Let me see whether the Christ in whom you believe will heal you.”
The saint said, “I believe in my Lord Jesus Christ: even if you inflict many punishments on me, you will not be able to shake me.”
For he said, “Do not fear those who will kill your body but have no power to kill your soul.
Instead, fear all the more the one who has the power to destroy your soul and your body in the fiery hell.”
Then the emperor ordered them to bring a red-hot piece of iron and place it beneath his private parts.
After that, they placed burning torches beneath his sides.
When they did this, instead of smoke, a powerful, sweet fragrance spread out to everyone in that place.
Although they tortured him still more, he neither groaned nor wept.
Decius said to him, “Where is your physician now? Let him come and heal you.
For you said, ‘He has the power to raise me if I die.’”
But Saint Mercurius said to him, “Do whatever you want.
You have authority over my body, but God is the master of my soul.
Even if you destroy my body, my soul will endure, remaining indestructible.”
Once again the emperor ordered them to hang him upside down and suspend a large stone from his neck, so that he would be strangled and die quickly.
But God's power and grace dwelt within the martyr, and he endured this torture for a long time.

When Decius saw that the martyr was enduring the punishments steadfastly and that no torture had affected him, he ordered them to remove that stone from his neck, bring a copper whip with four lashes, and beat him until the ground was soaked with his blood.
But the brave man was like a stone of adamant. He stood firm under this torture and said, “I thank you, my Lord, because you have made me worthy to suffer for your holy name.”

When the emperor saw that his resolve was unchanging and that he would not be able to persuade him to offer sacrifice, he took counsel, for he was in a hurry to go to Rome. He pronounced sentence on him, ordering him to be put to death by the sword, and said, “Mercurius has insulted the gods and despised the sacred decree of [?], treating it as nothing. Our authority commands that he be beheaded in the region of Cappadocia, there in that place, with everyone watching him.

For anyone who has received honor from the emperor and then opposes his command will be beaten and finally handed over to the sword.” Those appointed to take him away lifted him up, put him on a beast of burden, and tied him onto it, because the martyr's body had fallen apart everywhere and had become like a corpse.
They traveled along a long road, and within a few days they reached the city of Caesarea. Then they gently lowered him to the ground.
The Lord stood over him and said to him, “Mercurius, come and rest beside me, because you have completed your course and kept the faith.
Receive your crown of victory, which has been appointed for you to inherit.”

When the Lord appeared to the martyr, he gained strength. He said to those beside him, “Quickly do what you have been commanded to do. May the Lord, who calls everyone to repentance, make you worthy of his grace.
For he is rich and freely bestows gifts, without grudging, on those who turn to him.”
When he had said these things, they beheaded him, and he completed the good confession of our Savior on the twenty-fifth day of the month of November, which is Hathor.
Then a great miracle occurred, worthy of being remembered.
After the martyr had completed his martyrdom, his body became as white as snow, giving off a fragrance like choice lilies and fragrant resin.
Because of this sign, many people became Christians.
They laid the saint in a public place, where many miracles and healings take place.
To the glory of God the Father, his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, and the Holy Spirit forever. Amen.
The miracle revealed through Saint Mercurius: how he struck down Julian, the lawless emperor, with his spear. This miracle was recorded in the ninth book of the Church History. Amen.
At that time Cyril was bishop of Jerusalem, and a great sign of Christ appeared.
From the third hour of the day until the ninth hour, a great cross of light appeared, standing above the Savior's tomb, in the sight of everyone: believers and unbelievers, barbarians and Romans.
As a result, all the crowds in the cities stopped eating and drinking and left their wine, and [?] the cross until it went up into heaven [?] at the ninth hour.
Everyone's eyes were watching it.
Cyril, the bishop of Jerusalem, wrote about the miracle that had occurred. He wrote a letter and sent it to Emperor Constantius at the imperial court. He was the one who loved Athanasius.
Athanasius governed the church of Alexandria for another twenty-five consecutive years, and no conflict arose against him. For he had spent twenty-two years in the episcopate and in exile.
When Constantius died, Julian became emperor in his place.
He was a lawless pagan, born of the sister of Constantine the Great, for her husband was a pagan.
Constantine's sons saw that the young boy was insolent. They were afraid that he might seize [?] the kingdom while their [?] was still young. They handed him over to the church and made him a reader.
His father's people brought him up in paganism. When Constantius died, Julian became emperor in his place.
He immediately gave himself over to paganism and sought to open the temples publicly.
He stayed in the palace at Antioch, for he was not worthy to live in Constantine's residences.

He went to the place of the pagans and their idols. He took a falcon and gave it to the priest, who offered it as a sacrifice to the demon. The priest took the liver and gave it to him, and he ate it.
Julian was his sister's son, and he appointed him to govern.
When he saw the [?] of his mother's brother, he seized Saint Theodoric, the priest and administrator of the church, and killed him. He then came and received an answer from Julian.
But he rejected it, saying, “You have troubled me. I do not want to kill them, lest they boast, ‘We became martyrs because of you.’
“Instead, when I return from Persia, I will establish a law for them: a yearly head tax of three gold coins for Christian commoners, but three ounces for a council member.”
While doing these things, he was oppressing the Christians in every way.

At that time, the church was rich in the strength of those who bore the Spirit. Four pillars stood supporting it: Athanasius of Alexandria, Anthony and Pachomius in Upper Egypt, and Basil in Cappadocia.
Basil was Julian's friend because of the childhood they had spent together in Anzebe.
When he heard about his evil deeds, he went to him with other servants of God who were companions of his bishop.
When they went in to him, he saw that their appearance was humble and that their beards had grown long. He said to them, “What are these men looking for?”
Basil answered, “We are looking for a shepherd who is a good caretaker.”
He said to Basil, “Where did you leave the carpenter’s son when you came here?”
He said to him, “I left him making a coffin into which you will be thrown.”
The emperor said to him, “If I were not practicing philosophy because you are my friend, I would have your head cut off.”

Basil said to him, “You have not practiced philosophy. For if you had practiced philosophy, you would not have abandoned the wisdom you were taught when you were a reader of the books of true wisdom.”
The emperor said to him, “I have read them and understood them.”
Basil said, “You have not read them properly, nor have you ever understood them. For if you had understood them, you would not despise them.”
The emperor said to them, “I will imprison you until I return from Persia, so that you may learn what it means to oppose the emperor and have your fill of the misery of prison.”
Basil said, “If you go to Persia, you will not return; otherwise God has not spoken through Basil.”
The emperor Julian said, “What shall I do to that Galilean, that liar? For he said in his heart, ‘They will not leave one stone on another in the temple of the Jews.’
“I, for my part, will rebuild it as an imperial undertaking and refute his lying words, so that people may know that he is a liar.”
He ordered Basil to be taken into the prison, together with the other two who were with him, and sent him to Persia.

He came to Jerusalem and saw the ruins of the temple, with not a single wall surrounding it, just as Vespasian had destroyed it in the destruction he brought upon the Jews. He ordered it to be cleared so that they could rebuild it more splendidly than before.
Julian appointed a count over the temple to clear it, lay its foundation, and rebuild it.
He himself set out for Persia and waged war, leaving the holy ones confined in prison.
Those demolishing the temple cleared it and left no stone upon another. They did not dismantle it, according to the word of our Savior.
They began building. They would build from morning until evening, but when morning came, they would find the structures they had built demolished, though not by a human hand.
They spent two months continuing in this way, laboring without any lasting result, since providence was hindering them.
The Jews there told them, “Burn the tombs in which the Christians bury their dead, and you will be able to build.” They listened to them and burned the tombs.
But when they reached the tomb containing John the Baptist and Elisha the prophet, the fire did not touch them.
For many days the fire burned all around them, but the fire did not touch them.

Some of the brothers gave him money and begged him to allow them to take the bones of the holy ones. He accepted the money and did as they had asked him. He arranged for them to come at night and take the bones of the holy ones, John the Baptist and Elisha the prophet.
The Lord’s hand was with them. They wrapped them up to take them to Egypt to Athanasius, because he greatly desired to see them.

They went out to the sea and happened to find a ship. They boarded it, reached Alexandria without difficulty, and gave them to Athanasius. When he saw them, he rejoiced over them as though he had seen them in the flesh.
He hid them in the baptistery while looking for an opportunity to build a shrine for them.
One day he was eating in our fathers’ garden with the brothers. For every day he would invite the leading members of the clergy and eat with them—those who came to him on business.
They were not only eating, but also listening to the words of the wisdom that God had given him, as it is written: “Everything for the glory of God.”
Whether it was a time for fasting or a time for eating and drinking, he was always eating and drinking from the word of God.

He was eating with the brothers, the clergy, and the chief workers of the church in the garden he owned on the bank, called Hermes, south of the city. It opened onto rubbish heaps and deserted open spaces.
He said, “When I find the time, I will clear away the rubbish heaps and build the shrine of John the Baptist there.”
At that time Theophilus stood at the table while he was eating, because he was his secretary. He heard what Athanasius said and kept it in his heart.
Julian, following what drove him to go to Persia in anger, was handed over to the Persians by Christ Jesus, God, because he had left the saints imprisoned and gone to Persia.
This was how he died: at night he saw a crowd of soldiers coming against him out of the air. Then a spear struck him in the flanks, and he recognized that they were the saints.
He then took his blood and threw it up toward heaven, saying, “Take it for yourself, Jesus! You have taken over the whole place.”
For as soon as he blasphemed, he immediately fell, and God set his people free and saved us. [?] Romans to their place.
Three days before Julian’s death, Basil saw a dream in his sleep.
He awoke and told his two brothers, saying, “Tonight I saw the holy martyr, Saint Mercurius,
who had entered his shrine and drawn out his spear, saying, ‘Am I going to leave this lawless man like this, blaspheming the God of heaven?’”
When he had said these things, he went away, and I could no longer see him.
The other two answered, “Indeed, we too saw this same vision.”

When they saw this decision that God had revealed to them, they believed. They said to one another, “Let us send to the shrine of Saint Mercurius and see whether his spear is planted in its place or not.”
So they sent, and they did not find it. They believed the vision.
After three days, letters were sent to Antioch saying that the emperor had died in the war.
The entire senate, by God’s decree, took Jovian and made him emperor in Julian’s place.
He was a faithful man, devoted to God since childhood. He immediately released the saints: Basil, the pillar of truth, the Cappadocian, and the brothers.
And so Julian did not return, in accordance with Basil’s words.
In the peace of God. May the prayers and supplications of the great commander, Saint Mercurius, come upon us, so that we may all be saved together. 99.
The Martyrdom of Saint Mercurius, the Commander. He completed his glorious struggle on the twenty-eighth day of this month, Hathor, in the peace of God. May his holy blessings be with us. Amen.
It happened in the twelfth year of Emperor Decius, Valerian, and Maximian, when he was Caesar and emperor, that he stirred up a persecution against them all and everyone who professed Christ.
He issued a decree in every city, territory, and province, requiring every race of people [?] to sacrifice to the gods [?] throughout the entire inhabited world at that time.

These are the words written in this decree: “Decius Valerian Maxentius, the great sovereign emperor who rules over the whole inhabited world, writes throughout the inhabited world, the territories, and the provinces under my rule. [?] necessary [?] victory [?] the gods who reveal their honor to us, as they care for us through their goodwill, especially the great victory of this triumph which they grant us in war, rescuing us from our enemies who rise against us from time to time, so that the Roman dominion may receive glory everywhere, while the barbarians submit to us. [?]”

Immediately he came to pull him off the animal, intending to strike the poor laborer.

Immediately Saint Mercurius moved inside the coffin, and the mule on which he was mounted went backward. One of his feet hung down in the mule’s saddle. The mule did not stop running with him as he hung [?] blind.

The mule took on a human voice and cried out, saying, “You misguided people and pagans, whose [?] destroyed their god [?], come out and see the martyr Saint Mercurius and [?] your son, and believe in Jesus Christ, the God of heaven and earth.”
Again the mule ran with him, and [?] as it went around [?].
Oh, how great was the wonder and the spectacle that took place that day!
Not a single person in the whole city remained, whether [?] or great, [?] they came before the holy martyr, as though a power were driving them along.
The man himself, his wife, and his children were running after the mule. They were distressed
with him.
She took the golden idol she worshiped, broken into pieces, and came out into the middle of the city, while everyone watched her and her idol.
Her daughter led her like those who are blind, while she cried out, “Saint Mercurius, look at my humiliation, my great shame, and the shame of my idol, and have mercy on me!”

When she came out, her daughter told her, “[?] holy [?] in the coffin.” She cried out, “Martyr who received the crown from Christ the King, forgive me, and I will believe in you and your God, whose name I am not worthy to utter with a defiled mouth.”
Immediately a white watery film flowed down from her eyes as she wept. At once she could see, and her sight was restored as it had been before.
Afterward she took the pieces of the idol and smashed them against one another. She cried out, “Apollo has been put to shame! Christ and his martyr have received honor!”

When her parents saw the healing that had happened to their daughter, they cried out, “We are Christians! [?] is the God of heaven, together with his holy martyr, Saint Mercurius. Glory to him forever and ever. Amen.”

After these things, the Christian people spoke to one another, saying, “Let us take the martyr’s body into the city.” Others answered, “Perhaps the righteous man will not agree.”
After this they began to quarrel with one another. Immediately the righteous man moved by himself and went into the city.
The mule cried out, “Sing praise to the martyr!”

The father of the little boy who was hanging from the mule’s saddle cried out, saying, “I beg you, my lord the martyr: just as you gave light to my daughter, let your mercy also reach my other child, for he has suffered while hanging down.”
Immediately the martyr lay down on the ground, then rose and stood up, with no injury to his body, not even a burn. He had felt nothing at all.
The clergy and the devoted workers sang psalms before him, with burning lamps, choice incense, and fragrant branches, until they brought him into the city.
The man wanted to take him into his house, but the righteous man would not consent. His body became as heavy as lead, and they could not move him at all.

The crowd cried out, “He will not consent! Instead, let us take him to the church.” He yielded to them, and they took him to the church. They left him there until they could build a martyr’s shrine for him, according to his [?] worthiness. Glory to him forever and ever. Amen.
The Fourth Miracle of Saint Mercurius

After seven days, while all the people of the city were eating and drinking and celebrating with great joy because the saint's body had been revealed, the father of the little girl whose sight the saint had restored went to the bishop and asked for holy baptism.
He prescribed days of fasting for him. Afterward, he baptized him and his entire household in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
They counted the members of his family who had received the light of baptism with him. They found that fifty-three people had been baptized.
After all these things, [?] Saint Mercurius appeared to the poor man as before. He said to him, “Why are you sleeping and remaining idle? Have you not gotten up to make bricks for my shrine?”
The man said to him, “My lord, [?] I am poor. I have no workers, no livestock, and no money for expenses.”
The saint said to him, “I will give you everything you need. Only remain a poor man devoted to my house, and do not be of two minds. Then you will see my miracles.”
When you rise early, come east to the city's first canal. You will find the little boy whom the mule injured because he wanted to strike you on account of my body.
“Tell him, ‘Give me what you have, because I need it.’
And he will give you three gold coins, wishing to give them as a charitable offering.
“Only, I will not let you lack anything. They will bring you so much that you will not know what to do with it.
“If he asks you, ‘How did you find out that I have anything?’ tell him, ‘Mercurius, the one who healed you,
“‘is the one who told me to say this to you.’
“He should also say to his father, ‘You know that when you asked me, I quickly listened to you. I gave your daughter sight, and I also granted you your son safe and sound.

“‘If there is anything [?] still available, do good to your fellow martyr. For the honor of one companion over another, if it increases until morning, the excess beyond this is a burden on every side.’
“If he gives you work, do it. If he does not listen to you, buy yourself food with these three gold coins until I come to you, God willing. I am coming to you without delay.” These things
he said to him, and then departed from him in peace.

When morning came, the man got up and walked along the first street. He came upon the boy and received the three gold coins. He told him everything Saint Mercurius had said to him in the vision. The boy went and told his father in fear.
When his father heard these things, he gave glory to God and to his holy martyr, Saint Mercurius.

He did not neglect the matter at all. Instead, he harnessed his camels, hired many laborers, and provided a large sum for expenses. He gathered a great deal of material and put it into the poor man’s hands so that he could make bricks.
He also gave him the plow to till the ground, and everything else he needed.
One day, while the animals were plowing, one of them struck a thorn against one of the calves and tore its belly with its horns.

When the poor man saw what had happened, he was deeply distressed. He said, “Woe to me because of this! The man in authority has killed his animal. If only I had not told this boy about this vision so that he would tell his father! He will punish me for this deed, and this great sin will fall upon me.”

While he was saying these things, Saint Mercurius took on the appearance of a city official and came by. He saw the man and walked toward him, acting like someone who was astonished. He said to him, “Man, why did you leave the animals together until one injured the other?
For its owner will demand compensation from you for it.”
The laborer was deeply distressed, but he also gave glory to the God of Saint Mercurius.
The people who owned the animal heard about it and came to see what had happened to it. They were deeply grieved, because it was [?] in its beauty and strength.
Saint Mercurius was sitting at a distance, and no one saw him except the poor man.
A crowd of people gathered around the animal. They brought it into the city, to a place by itself, and gave it food to eat, but it did not taste any food at all.
Its owner was deeply distressed over it, because it was strong and physically fine.
When the people went to their homes, the poor man remained alone behind the animal, deeply distressed and thinking about his poverty.
Suddenly, Saint Mercurius came in, smiling with a holy smile, and stood beside the poor man’s animal, for he used to appear to him face to face.
He said to him with a laugh, “You did not take long to finish, brother!”
The man said to him, “Come and see what has happened to it.”
After this, Saint Mercurius nudged the calf with his foot and said to it, “In the name of Jesus Christ, my Lord, get up and do your work without illness.”
It rose with great strength, as though it had never been injured at all, and ate some of the grass.

Immediately Saint Mercurius rebuked the calf that had been fighting, saying to it, “Your horns will break off, along with your head. You will never again be able to gore any person or animal, but you will remain tame forever.”
Immediately his hair came loose, fell out, and separated from his head, and he fell into a state of [?].
The poor man bowed down before Saint Mercurius, saying to him, “Thank you for your small favor, my lord, martyr of Christ Jesus, you who suffered martyrdom for his holy name.”
Immediately Saint Mercurius disappeared from his sight.
The man went out rejoicing and shouting, “Saint Mercurius appeared to me! He healed the calf and rebuked the calf that had been fighting, and it became well behaved!”
A crowd came to see what had happened, and they all cried out, “The God of Saint Mercurius is one! Glory to him forever and ever! Amen.”
THE FIFTH MIRACLE OF SAINT MERCURIUS
After this, they began making bricks for the sanctuary of Saint Mercurius. A pagan official came over to the laborers who were making bricks for the sanctuary of Saint Mercurius.

He too quickly established his brickworks near them, since he also wanted to build a courtyard in his house. One day he came and sat beside the laborers who were working. He got up and inspected the bricks until he came upon the saint's bricks, and he desired the saint's bricks more than all his own.
He said, “Indeed, I will take a hundred and twenty bricks from these Christians’ bricks and tell the laborers that they made them for me.”
And if they say, ‘We will not let you take them away,’ I will beat them and carry them off by force, and see what this fellow called Mercurius will do to me.
He went home that day.

A few days later, he went and looked at the saint’s bricks. He sighed deeply, because the people of the city, small and great alike, were each sending a laborer every day to work, since they wanted to build a martyr’s shrine for him.
Then the pagan man became intensely envious of the saint’s bricks, with a great envy inspired by the devil.
After this, he called the poor man to whom Saint Mercurius had appeared. He said to him, “Come and tell me the quantity of my bricks and lime, because I want to build my house.”
The man said to him, “Your people know the number of your bricks.”
He said, “I do not take anyone with me except you. But in my own mind, these are mine [?].”

But the man [?]. He said to him, “Man, do not harm your soul. Do not touch this holy man's bricks, lest punishment overtake you. But if you take them, I will find out how strong and powerful you are.” And the pagan mocked the poor man.

He said to him, “You just said that that man would strike you. I will take even more than these, so that I can find out your strength and his, and what he will do to me.” The man said to him, “Do as you please. Look, the God of Saint Mercurius sees you, but you will not overcome him.”
The man immediately sent a slave of his, with great arrogance. He went and brought camels, and the man walked ahead of them with great arrogance.

He began loading the camels with the holy man's bricks. He stood in front of a large male camel that belonged to him and, with great arrogance, ordered his slaves to load the camels with bricks. He said, “Let me now see the power of this man called Mercurius.”
Immediately, before the words had left his mouth, a camel standing in front of him opened its mouth, seized the pagan governor, threw him down beside it, and lay down on him.

And the man cried out, saying, “My lord Saint Mercurius, forgive me for my ignorance. And all my bricks

When he had said these things, the camel set him down on the ground. And Saint Mercurius touched his wounds, healed him, and released him, with no wound anywhere on his body.
And great fear overtook everyone standing there who had seen how the camel had struck him.
And the man declared to them, “I saw Saint Mercurius piercing me with a spear.” Then he examined the man's body, but they found no wound anywhere on it.
They asked him, “Where is the wound on your body, especially since you were crying out, ‘Look, the righteous man is piercing my foot with his spear’?”
The man said to them, “Since the moment the camel released me and he touched my whole body, I have been well.”
And immediately the man went to the bishop, who baptized him and his entire household. And he released all his slaves as free people.
And he gave all the materials he had gathered for building his house, together with the timber, the stones, and all his bricks.
And he donated them to the sanctuary, together with fine gold and a large sum for expenses.
And he worked with his own hands, together with all his men and his livestock, all working without payment.
And he would say to the workers, “Go on and build the house of this mighty man.”
And he died, as is the appointed lot of every person, before they completed the shrine.
Glory to God and his holy martyr, Saint Mercurius.
The Sixth Miracle of Saint Mercurius
Now, when they began building the shrine of Saint Mercurius, they did so with great diligence, for there were abundant materials and many people working on the holy man's sanctuary.
After this, a man from the city came passing by. He saw the timber at the martyr’s shrine and was amazed. He wanted a piece of wood that was lying there.
He said, “I need this piece of wood, and I will take it.”
He went over to the wood, loaded it onto himself, and walked with it until he had gone a short distance into the city.

Then he became lost and did not know where he was going, because the saint had confused his mind, until he came and stood at the door of the poor man who was the caretaker of Saint Mercurius’s shrine.
This was the man to whom the saint used to appear. The other man did not know where he was going.

And behold, the saint spoke to the caretaker, saying to him, “What are you sitting there doing? Look, the timber at my sanctuary has been stolen! Get up and go to the door of your house. You will find the man with this piece of wood loaded onto him, lost and not knowing where he is going. For I am the one who confused him. I did not let him know where he was going until he came here, so that you would see him with the wood he stole loaded onto him.”
When he saw the house, and it was opened for him, he recognized the man as the steward of the martyr’s shrine. His senses returned to him.
Immediately he cried out, “The God of Saint Mercurius is one! Have mercy on me! Do not be angry with me and bring harm upon me, for I have sinned against you and stolen your timber.”

Then the saint again said to his caretaker, “Say this to the man: ‘Why do you not come and do a day’s work at my sanctuary? [?] wood that he donated to my sanctuary as an offering for the salvation of their souls—you went and stole it! But because of God’s mercy, look, I have forgiven you. Take the wood and put it back in its proper place, and go to your house.’ When he gets up in the morning, let him proclaim what he has done, so that the others will be afraid and will not steal the timber at my sanctuary again, lest I bring harm upon them.”
When he had said these things, he hid himself from him.
The poor man got up and came outside. He found the man with the wood loaded onto him, standing at the door of his house, not knowing where he was going.
He was saying, “Saint Mercurius, have compassion on me and have mercy on me, for I have sinned, my lord!”

The poor man spoke to him: “My dear brother, where are you coming from with the wood loaded onto you? I tell you, this wood belongs to Saint Mercurius. Now tell me everything that has happened to you.”
The man told him how he had taken the wood and how Saint Mercurius had confused his mind until he came to the door of the poor man’s house, unaware of where he was.
The man to whom Saint Mercurius [?] passed on to the man who had taken the wood every word that Saint Mercurius had spoken to him.

When the man heard these things, he was amazed and said, “Not just one [?] day! If the God of Saint Mercurius grants me safety, I will not stop working at his sanctuary until it is completed. And I will proclaim his power everywhere I go.”
Immediately he recovered his composure and went to his house, glorifying God and his holy martyr. He slept until morning.
When daylight came, he proclaimed throughout the whole city what had happened to him.
He went to the place from which the wood came, loaded it onto his neck while everyone watched him, and carried it to the saint’s sanctuary. He put it in the place from which he had taken it.
Great fear fell upon everyone who saw him, and they did not touch any other property belonging to the sanctuary again until it was completed.
And the man did not stop working, laying bricks for the saint’s sanctuary, until they had completed it.
And he was giving glory to the God of Saint Mercurius.
The Seventh Miracle of Saint Mercurius
Listen again, my beloved, to another great wonder, to the glory of God and Saint Mercurius.
Now, when they had beautifully constructed the sanctuary with every kind of craftsmanship, they fitted it with a wooden screen made of persea wood.
For the woman to whom Saint Mercurius had given sight owned three large persea trees, which her blessed husband had designated before his death. She had them as a large [?].
Then God [?] visited him, according to the fate appointed for everyone. He died and left her a great deal of property.
Then they fashioned an extremely beautiful arch of persea wood.

And when they had gathered the crowds to raise it, a few of the workers said to one another jokingly, “If only Saint Mercurius were pleased with us for building him a martyr’s shrine, and would make this arch of persea wood produce abundant fruit, as though it were rooted, so that we could eat from it!”
But suddenly, while the words were still coming out of their mouths, the wood put out branches laden with fine, ripe persea fruit.
And when the crowds saw what had happened, they cried out loudly, glorifying God and his holy martyr, who performs these miracles and these many wonders.
And some devoted people took away some of the fruit and kept it in their homes as a protection.
Oh, how many healings came about through that fruit! The crowds ate and were satisfied, and they thanked God and his holy martyr, Saint Mercurius.

Everyone in the city and its surrounding area heard about it, young and old alike. They all came together to see the great wonder. Men and women came to look at what had happened, which the righteous man had done.
There was also a Jew in the city called Gaipius. He was savage [?] toward everyone, but especially toward the Christians.
He too heard about the great wonder that had happened in the saint’s sanctuary. He said, “I will go and see whether these things the Christians are saying are true or not. Perhaps they are lying.”
He immediately gave orders to a slave of his to saddle a white female mule for him. He mounted it and said to his slave, “Come, let us see the ridiculous thing the Christians are doing.”
Then they traveled together until they came to the sanctuary of Saint Mercurius. The Jewish man went inside, mounted on his animal.
One of the young Christian boys working on the sanctuary said to him, “Where are you going, you godless man, bringing this animal into God’s church?”
But the Jewish man paid no attention to him at all. Instead, he went on, stopped, and looked up at the arch, laden with fruit and leaves as though it were rooted in the ground.
And the Jewish man said, “Who put these leaves from elsewhere on the crowns, lying about the saint by saying that he did this?”

The innocent little boy who had spoken earlier about the animal he was riding answered him, “The one who will strike you this very hour is the one who reveals all the wonders.” Immediately the man was filled with anger and great fury, and he drove the animal at the little boy, intending to strike him.
And immediately the mule’s feet sank down into the ground as though it were mud. He fell on his face and injured himself on the stones and bricks lying scattered at the building site.
And immediately, Saint Mercurius came in through the door, with an angel walking beside him and his spear in his hand.

He said to him, “What are you doing here, you senseless man? This is not a place for grazing. You have let your horse come in. These trees and fruits belong to other people. And you came here to beat those working at my shrine. You did not work, nor did you let those who were working do their work.”
Immediately he thrust his spear into the middle of the man's heart, and his intestines came out of him. No one could see the saint except the Jewish man whom the saint had struck.
But they saw the man lying stretched out, unconscious. They did not know what had happened to him.

Afterward the man cried out in a loud voice, saying, “Saint Mercurius, help me in this hour of distress! I will never again continue [?] anything belonging to the saint. And if you have mercy on me and free me from this affliction, I too will become a Christian, and I will erect your monument. I [?] you now in your glory, with your spear piercing me. I will also make an image of myself lying stretched out beneath your feet in great shame and helplessness. I will gild your image with fine gold and fiery-colored stones, namely chrysolite. And I will have the representation of your spear inlaid with genuine diamonds. Help me, my lord Mercurius!”
When he had said these things, he was lying stretched out, half dead.

After this, the angel of the Lord spoke to Saint Mercurius: “Withdraw your spear from him, if he is going to believe in our true King, Christ. A sinner is better than a righteous person who is going to sin. There is joy among the angels over a sinner when he repents of his sins, just as the Savior told his disciples. Leave him alone. Let your mercy reach him, for he is ignorant.”
And the saint released him.
When he came to his senses, he told the assembled crowd everything that had happened to him. They glorified God, who performs these miracles through his holy martyr.
After this, the man got up and went to his house, telling his wife and his servants everything that had happened to him. He had no children, because his wife was barren. On the following day,
he said to his wife, “Let whoever loves God follow me.”
And he took his wife and his servants and went to the bishop, who baptized them in the name of the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.
And he named him Zechariah, and his wife Elizabeth.
And when he went to his house, he had intercourse with his wife, and she conceived two male children at once.
And when the nine months were completed, she gave birth to twin children.
She named the firstborn Mercurius, after the saint, because they had obtained salvation through him. They named the second John, after the Baptist.
After all this, he summoned a craftsman and gave him ten pounds of fine gold and precious gemstones. He made the image of Saint Mercurius with his spear in his hand, and had it inlaid with diamonds.
And he also had his own image made of gold and precious stones, beneath Saint Mercurius, who was striking him in the heart with his spear.
And he brought his image into the church. After the consecration of the shrine, he placed it in front of the sanctuary, where it remains to this day.
And they now stand as a testimony to the miracles of the holy martyr, Saint Mercurius, in the peace of God. Amen.
The Eighth Miracle of Saint Mercurius
Now it happened that, after they had consecrated the saint's shrine, the news of the miracles reached everywhere.
And a great crowd was coming to his holy relics and bowing down before them. The sick received healing and went back to their homes.
