There was an official in a village near this place [?]. The name of that official was Lord Hermapollon.
He had a little daughter, his only child. He had never fathered any children except her.
He had left her a little orphan, and he watched over her as though he were looking at God.

He heard about the miracles of Saint Mercurius. He got up and took a small offering, amounting to thirty gold coins, and went to the saint’s shrine. He prayed and gave the thirty gold coins to the steward of the shrine.

The clergy urged him strongly to stay, for those clergy were hospitable people. Then they drank a great deal of wine and ate a great deal of food, entertaining the official. Then a conversation arose among them.
The official said, “What do you need? Tell me, so that I can provide it for this shrine.”
The clergy and the steward said to him, “We want a fine resting place on which to lay the martyr’s body.”

The official answered, saying, “If the God of Saint Mercurius fulfills this request of mine, I will prepare a resting place for the martyr and cover it with precious ivory, like those belonging to the Roman emperors.”

After this, the official went to sleep that night. Saint Mercurius appeared to him in the form of a military commander and said to him, “When you get up, mount your animal and go home. Do not delay in preparing this couch, as you said you would. For I know that you will be somewhat negligent about the arrangements for the resting place that the clergy told you about this evening. But I will not hold you to account. I know that after some time you will hurry to come to my shrine, and I will have mercy on you.”
The official awoke from the vision and was greatly amazed.
When morning came, he went to the church and bowed down before the martyr’s body. He came out, mounted his animals, and went home.

When a day had passed since the governor had come to the saint’s shrine, a governor of the city heard about his unmarried daughter, that she was very beautiful. He sent men from the city to him, saying, “I want to take your daughter as a wife for my son. Then the little girl’s mother, the official’s wife, called him and told him about the matter.

Then the official’s wife told everything to the women who had come. They went away distressed and told the young man and his parents what had happened. They were grieved and said nothing.

Within a month of these events, the young man’s mother died. Because of the grief over his mother, his father did not look for another woman for him.
But the thought of the girl did not stop troubling the young man. He declined day by day until he came close to death.

The saint said to him, “I am Mercurius, who performs miracles in this city, Caesarea. As soon as morning came, he hurried to my father and said to him, “My father, help me, for I wish to go to the shrine of Saint Mercurius and pray.”

His father cherished him greatly, because he had no one besides him. He said, “Go, my son, but do not delay your return and leave my heart burning with longing for you, light of my eyes.” He also gave him a large sum for expenses and three male servants to travel with him.
Then he set out on the road in great haste, coming to the city where the magician lived.
He said to him, “Get up. Let us go to the shrine of Saint Mercurius and pray.” And he told the magician everything that had happened to him.

When the magician heard that [?] the man and his daughter were at the saint’s shrine, he became afraid. The magician said, “Even if I am summoned now, I will not come to the shrine of Saint Mercurius, lest he expose me and the girl’s father kill me because of his daughter.”

Immediately the young man hurried with great force until he reached the saint’s shrine. In great fear, he bowed down over the saint’s body. He saw the girl lying over the saint’s body, with her father and mother begging him to help her.
The saint was leaving her for a favorable [?]. The young man called the steward and gave him ten gold coins.

The governor, who was the girl’s father, looked [?] and saw the young man. He recognized him and approached him, knowing nothing about the matter. He greeted him and asked him about the well-being of his household.
When the two of them had prayed, he invited the young man and took him to the place upstairs where he was staying. They ate and drank together. When he saw the girl, he was very glad.

He was also distressed about her because she was suffering, and he felt ashamed before her parents because [?] her illness. He was also afraid that the martyr would expose him. In short, there were many worries in the young man’s heart.

Saint Mercurius appeared to the girl’s father. He woke him while he was sleeping and took him outside the place where he slept. He addressed him: “Give your daughter to the young man who is with you, if you want me to heal her for you. And do not seek to harm him, lest another affliction strike her, worse than this one.”

He also told him, “There are three more [?] until his father passes away, for his lifetime has reached its end. And do not neglect to give him your daughter after his father’s death.” He told him how the young man had used magic on his daughter, causing her to become ill because of his desire for her. He also told him how he had appeared to the young man and threatened him to make him stop, and about everything that had happened to the young man until he came to the shrine.
After Saint Mercurius had said these things, he disappeared from his sight. The governor awoke from the vision and smelled a strong, exquisite fragrance.
He said, “Truly, it was Saint Mercurius who came and appeared to me.”
He continued reflecting on what the young man had done to his daughter because of his desire for her. He kept pondering, “Does the saint want me to reveal the secret, or should I keep it hidden?”

While he was thinking about these things, a trumpet was sounded so that everyone who was sleeping would get up, come to the church, and sing hymns with the devotees [?]. For it was the saint’s great festival, on the twenty-fifth of Hathor. The crowds got up, joyfully dressed in white, and came to the church.
They continued singing hymns until daylight spread.

The man also got up and called his wife and daughter. They came to the shrine, with their servants following them. The young man also came with his servants. They went and bowed down over the saint’s body.
They were rejoicing. The young man searched the sleeping quarters, marveling at their beauty. He found the magician tied to the martyr’s ring [?], like a dog, keeping silent.
When he saw the young man, he cried out, “Woe to me, my lord and brother! Come and see my great humiliation!”
The young man said to him, “Where did you come from to this place?”
The magician said to him, “Oh, my brother, after you left me, Saint Mercurius came to me. He put a muzzle on me, brought me here, and bound me inside this sleeping place, to my shame.”
Immediately he cried out, “Help me, my beloved brother! While I was speaking with you, the saint slapped me in the face, and I have been terribly humiliated.”
He said to him, “You were not told about a mystery in order to reveal it. Why are you going to seek it out to reveal it?”

And immediately a demon sprang upon the magician, untied him, and threw him onto the ground, crying out, “Let me punish him! Saint Mercurius is the one commanding me, because the blasphemies he has uttered against the God who created him are great.”
And a demon also threw a woman down beside the saint’s body.
When they dismissed the congregation, the whole crowd gathered, watching how the saint humiliated the demons.
And the governor himself also came and sat down.

The demon-possessed woman cried out, “Oh, Hermapollon, and [?] the evil of this magician, for he has bewitched your daughter. His wife was bewildered by what she heard. And at that very moment [?], her daughter was freed from her torment, as though she had never been ill at all.

The woman said to the magician, with Saint Mercurius speaking through her, “From this moment you must not live among people. Instead, you must flee to the mountains and practice ascetic discipline alone in the wilderness until the day of your death.”
He rebuked the spirit within him and cast it out. His eyesight was fully restored, and he went into the wilderness and lived in seclusion until the day of his death.
When the feast day dawned, Hermapollon mounted his animals with his wife, his daughter, and his servants. The young man also came with his servants, and they returned to their city.
The governor told his wife everything the saint had said to him in the vision.
His wife realized that what the governor had told her about the vision was also what the saint had said through the mouth of the demon-possessed woman.
When the people heard, great unity of purpose arose among them. They sent and [?], and [?] with him.
They told him, “Take care of the arrangements so that we may celebrate the wedding just as Saint Mercurius told us.”
When the young man heard these things, he was very happy. When dinner was over, the young man went home and told his father everything. His father rejoiced even more.
Early the next morning, the young man’s father gathered all the wealthy leading men of the city. They came to the house of Lord Hermapollon and spoke with him about his daughter.
They reached an agreement with one another and gave her much gold and silver, many ornaments, male and female slaves, and ships that sailed on the sea.
They brought [?], tightrope walkers, organists, mime performers, flute players, and [?]. They celebrated the wedding with great splendor.
After another week, they invited many wealthy people and many governors. They celebrated the wedding with great worldly splendor and rejoiced greatly.
Within three months after the wedding, the young man’s father died at a very advanced age.

And when the days of his mourning were over, the young man took his gold, his silver, all his possessions, and his servants, and brought them to his father-in-law’s house. They stayed together until the day of their death.
And every year they came to the shrine of Saint Mercurius on his holy feast day, praying and giving thanks to God, the Lord of great powers.
And you have seen, my beloved, these great acts of grace that God performs with his chosen ones from time to time. I also wish, O God-loving people, to take a little from you.
But I know that no one can reach the end of the miracles of the saints, especially those of the martyr Saint Mercurius.
